strengths: Elegant and correct central theory: Observation 3.1 (Shapley values depend only on the odd component of the value function) is cleanly proven, and Theorem 3.2 rigorously shows paired sampling decouples the weighted least-squares objective into independent odd/even subproblems. Corollary 3.3 resolves an open conjecture from Fumagalli et al. (2026) about order-k paired-sampling fits being equivalent to order-(k+1), generalizing prior results that were limited to degree 2 (Mayer & Wüthrich, 2025). This is a genuine theoretical unification of a widely used heuristic.

The algorithmic design is well-motivated by the theory: switching from the unanimity basis to the Fourier basis (Lemma 3.4 shows span equivalence on T≤k) cleanly isolates odd basis functions, and the hybrid use of ProxySPEX for interaction screening plus sparse odd-constrained regression (with exact efficiency constraints derived in Appendix C) yields a consistent estimator with polynomial overhead (Eq. 15) instead of the O(d^2k) cost of PolySHAP.

Strong empirical evaluation against recent, relevant baselines (MSR, SVARM, Permutation Sampling, LeverageSHAP, RegressionMSR, 3-PolySHAP, Proxy LGBM) across 8 value functions spanning tabular, image, and language domains, with exact ground truth (exhaustive summation or exact interventional TreeSHAP). OddSHAP achieves the best average rank (1.50), and results are reported honestly—e.g., RegressionMSR wins on Estate, and performance parity with baselines in low-budget regimes is acknowledged.

Useful ablations: interaction-count ablation (Figure 4, 11) demonstrates the bias-variance tradeoff of sparsity (6x–62x error reductions with overfitting at η=2), runtime decomposition by algorithm component (Figure 6), and runtime-based comparisons under varying per-evaluation costs.

Good reproducibility practices: code in supplementary material, implementation details (LightGBM proxy settings, sampling via shapiq CoalitionSampler, hardware) documented, and limitations discussed candidly, including the observation that even components can carry useful information when even/odd interactions are correlated and that paired sampling increases mutual coherence.
weaknesses: The theoretical depth is modest: Observation 3.1 and the even-odd decomposition of the paired-sample objective (Theorem 3.2) follow from short algebraic arguments, and the consistency result (Theorem 3.5) is a straightforward composition of known results (Charnes et al. 1988 + projection tower property). No finite-sample error bounds or sample-complexity guarantees for OddSHAP are provided—consistency is only asymptotic (m → 2^d), which is far outside practical budgets.

The estimator's practical performance depends on the proxy-based interaction screening (GBT + ProxySPEX), which is not covered by the theory: the consistency guarantee applies to the regression stage given a support T, but the screening step can miss important interactions, and no guarantee connects the selected support to estimation error. The method is essentially a combination of existing components (ProxySPEX screening + Fourier-basis constrained regression).

Empirical scope is narrower than the framing suggests: although the introduction motivates feature importance, data valuation, and causal inference, experiments cover only local feature-attribution value functions, 30 explained instances per dataset, and d ≤ 101. 3-PolySHAP is only compared on 4 of 8 benchmarks, so the claimed superiority over higher-order polynomial methods is partially extrapolated rather than directly demonstrated.

Gains over the strongest baseline (RegressionMSR) are consistent but not uniform (e.g., Estate), and Table 1 shows some per-dataset losses; 'state-of-the-art' claims rest on average rank across a limited benchmark suite.

Presentation issues: duplicated/erroneous references (Lundberg et al. 2020a/b/c are the same paper; Strumbelj & Kononenko 2014 listed twice; arXiv:2601.18608 formatting), minor notation/typo slips ('IG60' vs. IL60, 'odd cardinality' phrasing), and Figure 1 is more decorative than informative. The non-uniqueness handling via Minkowski sums in Theorem 3.2/Corollary 3.3 deserves a more careful statement of when minimizers are unique.

strengths: The core observation (Shapley values depend only on the odd component of the value function, f_odd(S) = (f(S) − f(S^c))/2) is clean and correct, and it yields a genuinely general explanation for why paired sampling improves regression-based Shapley estimators, resolving an open conjecture from Fumagalli et al. (2026) that was previously only established for degree ≤ 2 interactions (Mayer & Wüthrich, 2025).

The theoretical development is self-contained and the proofs (Observation 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3, Lemma 3.4, Theorem 3.5) appear sound, including careful handling of non-unique minimizers via Minkowski sums and of exact boundary constraints in the Fourier domain (Appendix C).

The proposed OddSHAP estimator is a sensible combination of existing components (paired sampling, ProxySPEX-style GBT interaction screening, sparse odd-order Fourier regression) that retains consistency of polynomial regression while reducing the basis from combinatorial O(d^k) to budget-scaled |T| = d + ⌈m/η⌉, with a clearly stated runtime analysis.

Experiments cover 8 value functions spanning language, vision, and tabular domains (d = 14 to 101), with appropriate baselines (MSR, SVARM, Permutation Sampling, LeverageSHAP, RegressionMSR, 3-PolySHAP), median/IQR reporting, runtime ablations across per-evaluation costs, and an informative sparsity ablation that honestly shows overfitting when too many interactions are selected.

The limitations section is candid, noting that even/odd interactions can be correlated (so discarding even structure may lose signal) and that paired sampling increases mutual coherence; code is provided in the supplementary material and hyperparameters (η, L) are specified.
weaknesses: The central theoretical insight is elementary: Observation 3.1 is a direct complementary-pair cancellation argument, and Theorems 3.2/3.5 are short exercises in orthogonality and nested projections. Framing this as an 'elegant and fundamental' unification overstates the depth; the practical novelty is largely a careful recombination of paired sampling, ProxySPEX, and PolySHAP-style regression.

There are no finite-sample error bounds or guarantees for the full pipeline. Consistency holds only as m → 2^d with the candidate set ⌈m/η⌉ growing accordingly; at realistic budgets the interaction selection via the GBT proxy is heuristic, so the claimed consistency advantage over pure proxy methods is weaker than the narrative suggests.

Empirical support for 'state-of-the-art' is uneven. 3-PolySHAP is only evaluated on 4 of 8 datasets and beats OddSHAP by roughly three orders of magnitude on Estate (3.2×10⁻⁷ vs 6.1×10⁻⁵), which undercuts the headline claim; on low-dimensional tasks OddSHAP merely ties RegressionMSR. The average-rank summary partially obscures these per-dataset losses.

The evaluation is restricted to local model-prediction explanations with interventional marginal-expectation value functions (30 explained instances per benchmark, 50 background samples). The introduction motivates the work via data valuation and causal attribution, but neither is tested, and only MSE to ground truth is reported (no downstream utility of the attributions).

The method depends on hyperparameters (η governing |Todd|, tree depth L) whose sensitivity is shown qualitatively (Figure 4) but without principled guidance; performance degrades sharply for η = 2, and behavior for small m falls back to plain TreeSHAP on the proxy, i.e., to an unadjusted proxy estimator.

Presentation issues: inconsistent naming (IL60 appears as 'IG60' in Section 5.1), duplicated reference entries (Lundberg et al. 2020a/b/c, Strumbelj & Kononenko 2014 twice, Covert & Lee 2021a/b), and Table 1's ranking mixes methods evaluated on different subsets, which can mislead.

strengths: The central insight — that the Shapley value depends only on the odd component f_odd of the value function (Observation 3.1) — is correct, elegant, and verifiable (the cancellation over complementary pairs relies only on the symmetry p_{|S|-1} = p_{d-|S|}, which checks out).

Theorem 3.2 cleanly explains why paired sampling works: it orthogonalizes the regression objective into independent odd/even subproblems. This yields Corollary 3.3, which resolves an open conjecture of Fumagalli et al. (2026) about the equivalence of order-k and order-(k+1) fits under paired sampling for odd k. This is a genuine unification of prior fragmented results (Mayer & Wüthrich 2025; Fumagalli et al. 2026).

OddSHAP is a sensible, practical algorithm: using the Fourier basis (whose parity aligns with interaction order) to isolate the odd subspace, ProxySPEX for interaction screening, and exact boundary constraints for the efficiency property (Appendix C is a nice, careful derivation).

Experiments cover 8 value functions spanning d = 14 to 101 and multiple domains, with a broad set of strong baselines (LeverageSHAP, RegressionMSR, MSR, SVARM, Permutation Sampling, 3-PolySHAP), runtime ablations (Figures 5–6), simulated evaluation costs (Figures 7–10), and a sparsity ablation (Figures 4, 11). Median/IQR reporting is appropriate, and code is provided.
The limitations section is honest, explicitly noting the possible benefit of correlated even components and the increased mutual coherence induced by paired sampling.
weaknesses: The theoretical depth is modest: Observation 3.1 is a short algebraic identity, Theorem 3.2 is an elementary decomposition argument, and Lemma 3.4/Theorem 3.5 largely follow from known unanimity–Fourier conversions (Grabisch 2016) plus the projection argument in Fumagalli et al. (2026). The elegance of the insight somewhat outpaces its technical difficulty.

The state-of-the-art claim is somewhat overstated: in Table 1/3, RegressionMSR achieves lower MSE on DistilBERT (3.1e-5 vs 5.2e-5) and Estate (1.3e-5 vs 6.1e-5), and on ViT16 the two are comparable. OddSHAP's advantage is concentrated in moderate/high-dimensional settings with sufficient budget.

No finite-sample error guarantees are provided. Consistency holds only in the m → 2^d limit, and the odd-interaction support T_odd is chosen heuristically by a GBT proxy (ProxySPEX); if the proxy misses high-impact interactions, accuracy may degrade in ways the paper does not bound or analyze.

The evaluation uses only 30 randomly selected instances per value function, and 3-PolySHAP is only compared on 4 low-dimensional benchmarks; direct comparisons to original FourierSHAP/ProxySPEX configurations as published baselines are indirect (via the 'Proxy (LGBM)' variant).

The method is sensitive to the hyperparameter η: too small a value causes overfitting (Figure 4/11), and in the m < d·η regime the method degenerates to plain TreeSHAP on the GBT proxy, where the paper's core 'odd' insight plays no role. The acknowledged increase in mutual coherence from pairing is never quantified.
